title: The Audit
theme: An auditor arrives from the mainland: harden everything

missions.title: Nobody Runs as Root
missions.story:
AUDIT FINDING F-01
Auditor: Wren Achebe        Severity: HIGH

Observed: the process inside container `telemetry` runs as uid 0. A single bug in the telemetry parser would hand an attacker root inside that container, with every kernel feature root can reach.

Required: the service has no reason to be root. Recreate `telemetry` from `alpine:3.20` so it runs as user and group 1000:1000, and keep it running. I will check with `id`.

Remediation window: until the supply ship leaves Friday.
objectives: Remove the root-running container `telemetry`
Run a new container named `telemetry` from `alpine:3.20` with `sleep infinity`, in the background
It must run as user 1000 and group 1000
missions.startingState: A container `telemetry` (alpine:3.20, sleep infinity) is running as root.
hints: A container's user is chosen when it is created; you cannot turn a running root container into an unprivileged one. You have to replace it, and `docker run` has an option that sets the user and group the main process runs as.
The flag is `--user` (short form `-u`) and takes `UID:GID`. Remove the old container with `docker rm -f` first, because the name `telemetry` is taken.

```bash
docker rm -f telemetry
docker run -d --name telemetry --user 1000:1000 alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
docker exec telemetry id
```

commands: docker run -d --name telemetry alpine:3.20 sleep infinity

validation.description: Container `telemetry` is running from `alpine:3.20`
The container is configured to run as `1000:1000`
`id -u` inside `telemetry` prints 1000
`id -g` inside `telemetry` prints 1000

solution: docker run -d --name telemetry --user 1000:1000 alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
missions.debrief: Running as a non-root user means an exploited process starts with far fewer powers, and `--user UID:GID` achieves that without rebuilding the image. Pro tip: use a numeric UID:GID rather than a name, because names only resolve if the image has a matching /etc/passwd entry.

missions.title: Carved in Stone
missions.story:
[RADIO -- INGRID TO ENGINEER, 06:40]

Engineer, Halvorsen. Wren just showed me that anything that gets a shell inside `ledger` can rewrite the ledger program itself. Tomasz's ice-core sample counts run through that service; if the code can be tampered with, nobody can trust the numbers.

Rebuild the container so its root filesystem is read-only. The service still needs somewhere to write its running log, so give it a RAM-backed `/tmp` and nothing more. Same port as before, 8140. Over.
objectives: Replace container `ledger` with a new one from `python:3.12-alpine`, publishing host port 8140 to container port 8000
Mount `/workspace/app` read-only at `/app` and run `python /app/ledger.py`
Make the root filesystem read-only, with a `tmpfs` at `/tmp`
http://localhost:8140 must still answer
missions.startingState: Container `ledger` runs the service with a writable root filesystem; the code is in `/workspace/app/ledger.py`.
hints: Docker can start a container with its whole root filesystem mounted read-only, so nothing can be changed or installed. Programs that need scratch space then require a separate writable location, and RAM-backed temporary mounts are the usual answer.

Use `--read-only` for the filesystem and `--tmpfs /tmp` for the one writable path. A container cannot be edited in place, so remove `ledger` first and recreate it with the same port and bind mount (`-v /workspace/app:/app:ro`).

```bash
docker rm -f ledger
docker run -d --name ledger --read-only --tmpfs /tmp \
  -p 8140:8000 -v /workspace/app:/app:ro \
  python:3.12-alpine python /app/ledger.py
curl localhost:8140
```

files.content:
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

LOG = "/tmp/ledger.log"


class Ledger(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        with open(LOG, "a") as f:
            f.write("sample logged\n")
        with open(LOG) as f:
            entries = len(f.readlines())
        self.send_response(200)
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(f"LEDGER OK entries={entries}\n".encode())


HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8000), Ledger).serve_forever()

validation.description: Container `ledger` is running from `python:3.12-alpine`
The root filesystem of `ledger` is read-only
`/tmp` is mounted as a tmpfs
Writing to the root filesystem (`/etc`) fails
Writing to `/tmp` still works
http://localhost:8140 still answers with the ledger entry count

missions.debrief: With the root filesystem locked, an intruder cannot plant or alter a single binary, and `--tmpfs` still gives the service the scratch space it needs. Pro tip: when a program dies with 'Read-only file system', the error names the exact path that needs its own tmpfs or volume.

missions.title: Fewer Keys on the Ring
missions.story:
NORA: GATEKEEPER CAPABILITY COUNT 14
NORA: GATEKEEPER REQUIRED CAPABILITIES 1
NORA: AUDITOR WREN FLAGGED EXCESS PRIVILEGE

The `gatekeeper` container serves the crew login page on port 8150 and runs with Docker's default bundle of 14 Linux capabilities. Its only privileged act is binding to port 80 inside the container.

Wren's note, pinned beside the alert: "Least privilege is not a suggestion. Take every key off the ring, then hand back the one it needs." Recreate `gatekeeper` that way.
objectives: Replace container `gatekeeper` with one from `python:3.12-alpine`, publishing host port 8150 to container port 80
Run `python -m http.server 80 --directory /gate` with `/workspace/gate` mounted read-only at `/gate`
Drop ALL capabilities and add back only `NET_BIND_SERVICE`
The login page at http://localhost:8150 must still load
missions.startingState: Container `gatekeeper` is running with the default capability set; the login page lives in `/workspace/gate/`.
hints: Linux splits root's powers into separate capabilities, and Docker gives each container a default set of 14. You can remove capabilities when creating a container, and add specific ones back. Binding a port below 1024 is one such capability.

`--cap-drop ALL` removes the whole default set, and `--cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE` returns the single one the web server needs. The order of the flags does not matter, but the container has to be recreated.

```bash
docker rm -f gatekeeper
docker run -d --name gatekeeper \
  --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  -p 8150:80 -v /workspace/gate:/gate:ro \
  python:3.12-alpine python -m http.server 80 --directory /gate
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.CapAdd}}' gatekeeper
```

commands: docker run -d --name gatekeeper -p 8150:80 -v /workspace/gate:/gate:ro python:3.12-alpine python -m http.server 80 --directory /gate

validation.description: Container `gatekeeper` is running from `python:3.12-alpine`
All default capabilities are dropped (`CapDrop` contains ALL)
`NET_BIND_SERVICE` is added back
`NET_BIND_SERVICE` is the only capability added
The main process holds only the bind-service capability
The crew login page still loads on port 8150

solution: docker run -d --name gatekeeper --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE -p 8150:80 -v /workspace/gate:/gate:ro python:3.12-alpine python -m http.server 80 --directory /gate
missions.debrief: Capabilities slice root into small privileges, and dropping ALL then adding back one by name is the strictest form of least privilege Docker offers. Pro tip: if a dropped container fails, its error message names what is missing, so add capabilities back one at a time rather than reaching for `--privileged`.

missions.title: Rationing
missions.story:
Sticky note on monitor 3, Amara's handwriting:

"cruncher went into a loop at 3am, spawned a few hundred processes and took the whole box with it. sorry!!

can you box it in? 256 MB of RAM, half a CPU, 64 processes max.
DO NOT restart it -- the glacier job is 80% done and I wrote the checkpoint file by hand. -- A."

Beneath it, in red pen, Wren has underlined "whole box" twice.
objectives: Limit the running container `cruncher` to 256 MB of memory
Limit it to 0.5 CPUs
Limit it to at most 64 processes
Do not recreate it: `/tmp/checkpoint` inside the container must survive
missions.startingState: Container `cruncher` (alpine:3.20) runs with no limits at all, and holds a checkpoint in `/tmp/checkpoint`.
hints: Resource limits are not only for new containers; Docker can change them on a running one. Restarting or recreating `cruncher` would lose the checkpoint that only exists inside it, so look for a command that edits a live container.
`docker update` accepts `--memory`, `--cpus` and `--pids-limit`. When you set a memory limit on a container that had none, set `--memory-swap` to the same value so swap does not exceed it.

```bash
docker update --memory 256m --memory-swap 256m --cpus 0.5 --pids-limit 64 cruncher
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}} {{.HostConfig.PidsLimit}}' cruncher
```

commands: docker run -d --name cruncher alpine:3.20 sleep infinity

validation.description: Container `cruncher` is still running
Memory limit is 256 MB (268435456 bytes)
CPU limit is 0.5 CPUs
Process limit is 64
The original container (with its checkpoint) was not recreated

missions.debrief: Memory, CPU and process limits keep one runaway container from starving everything else on the host, and `docker update` applies them live without touching the container's state. Pro tip: `--pids-limit` is the cheap defence against fork bombs, and `docker stats` shows whether a limit is actually being hit.

missions.title: Secrets Belong in Files
missions.story:
**From:** Wren Achebe
**Subject:** F-05 -- credential visible to anyone who can run `docker inspect`

Engineer,

I ran `docker inspect uplink` and `docker history kestrel/uplink:1.0`. The satellite uplink's API key appears in plain text in both: it was baked into the image as an `ENV` line. Anyone who pulls this image owns the key.

Rebuild `kestrel/uplink:1.0` without it, and give the container the key as a read-only file at `/run/secrets/api_key`, taken from `/workspace/secrets/api_key.txt`. The program already knows how to read that file.

Rotating the key is Ingrid's job. Yours is making sure it is not in the image.

W.
objectives: Rebuild image `kestrel/uplink:1.0` from `/workspace` without the `API_KEY` environment variable in the image or its history
Replace container `uplink` with one from the new image, publishing host port 8160 to 8000
Bind-mount `/workspace/secrets/api_key.txt` read-only at `/run/secrets/api_key`
The container must not receive `API_KEY` as an environment variable
missions.startingState: `kestrel/uplink:1.0` was built with `ENV API_KEY=...` and container `uplink` runs on port 8160. The key file `secrets/api_key.txt` is ready.
hints: Anything in `ENV`, `ARG` or a `RUN` command becomes part of the image's metadata or history, and `docker inspect` shows a container's environment too. Secrets should arrive at runtime, as a file that is not part of the image.

Delete the `ENV API_KEY=...` line from the Dockerfile and rebuild the same tag. Then recreate the container with a bind mount of the key file onto `/run/secrets/api_key`, ending in `:ro`. Do not pass the key with `-e`.

```bash
sed -i '/^ENV API_KEY/d' Dockerfile
docker build -t kestrel/uplink:1.0 .
docker rm -f uplink
docker run -d --name uplink -p 8160:8000 \
  -v /workspace/secrets/api_key.txt:/run/secrets/api_key:ro \
  kestrel/uplink:1.0
```

files.content:
FROM python:3.12-alpine
WORKDIR /srv
ENV API_KEY=kp_live_9Q4xT2
COPY app.py .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

validation.description: The image's environment no longer contains `API_KEY`
The image history no longer contains the key value
Container `uplink` is running from `kestrel/uplink:1.0`
The container has no `API_KEY` environment variable
The key file is bind-mounted read-only at `/run/secrets/api_key`
The uplink authenticates using the mounted key

missions.debrief: Whatever you put in an image layer, `ENV` or `ARG` stays readable by anyone holding the image, so credentials belong in files mounted at runtime (Compose `secrets:` does the same thing). Pro tip: add secret paths to `.dockerignore` so they can never be copied in by accident, and rotate any key that was ever baked into an image.

missions.title: A Relay That Can't Escalate
missions.story:
**Kip:** quick question, what does USER do in a Dockerfile?

**Kip:** asking because Wren ran `docker run --rm --entrypoint id kestrel/safe-relay:1.0 -u` on my relay image and said a word I can't repeat in front of Ingrid. It printed 0.

**Kip:** she also wants the running container to have no-new-privileges, which I think means setuid tricks stop working? can you do the Dockerfile AND the container? Dockerfile and `relay.sh` are in /workspace. I'll watch and learn!
objectives: Edit the Dockerfile so image `kestrel/safe-relay:1.0` creates an unprivileged user and sets it with `USER`, then rebuild that tag
The image's default user must not be root
Replace container `relay` with one from the rebuilt image, started with `no-new-privileges`
The container's process must not run as uid 0
missions.startingState: `kestrel/safe-relay:1.0` was built from the Dockerfile in `/workspace` (no `USER` line); container `relay` runs from it as root.
hints: Without a `USER` instruction an image runs as root. Setting the user in the Dockerfile makes safe the default for everyone who runs the image, instead of relying on each person remembering a flag. The second requirement is a separate runtime setting, passed with `--security-opt`.

In the Dockerfile: create a user with Alpine's `addgroup -S` and `adduser -S`, then put `USER relay` before `CMD`. At runtime the option is `--security-opt no-new-privileges`. Rebuild the same tag and replace the old container.

```dockerfile
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN addgroup -S relay && adduser -S -G relay relay
COPY relay.sh /usr/local/bin/relay.sh
USER relay
CMD ["sh", "/usr/local/bin/relay.sh"]
```

Then build and run:

```bash
docker build -t kestrel/safe-relay:1.0 .
docker rm -f relay
docker run -d --name relay --security-opt no-new-privileges kestrel/safe-relay:1.0
```

validation.description: The image sets a default user (`USER` in the Dockerfile)
Running the image's default configuration does not give uid 0
Container `relay` is running from `kestrel/safe-relay:1.0`
`relay` was started with `no-new-privileges`
The process inside `relay` is not uid 0
The relay reports an unprivileged uid in its log

solution:
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN addgroup -S relay && adduser -S -G relay relay
COPY relay.sh /usr/local/bin/relay.sh
USER relay
CMD ["sh", "/usr/local/bin/relay.sh"]
EOF
missions.debrief: `USER` makes the safe choice the default for everyone who runs the image, and `no-new-privileges` stops setuid binaries from gaining more rights than the process started with -- two layers that work together. Pro tip: put `USER` after your `RUN` steps that need root (installing packages), so only the final runtime stage is unprivileged.
